text.p: Meekatharra Minerals Ltd will decide on construction of a demonstration plant for its US$500 million South Australian pig iron export project in the next six weeks, general manager Neil Arthur told Reuters.

The contract for construction of the plant will be awarded to BHP Engineering, a unit of The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd once costings were finalised, he said. BHP Engineering already has been selected to design and cost the demonstration plant, to be built near Whyalla, South Australia, Arthur said.
"We're hopeful that we can commit to the commercial plant around the end of 1998 or early 1999 so we'd be producing commercial product by around the turn of the century," he said.
Arthur was commenting on the role which Meekatharra might play in the economics of the proposed A$1 billion Alice Springs-Darwin railway.

The Northern Territory (NT) government will present a new submission on the proposed 1,410 km railway, which would open Australia's northernmost city of Darwin to major new export trade to Asia, to the federal government later this month.

In a recent interview with Reuters in Darwin, Barry Coulter, the territory's minister for transport and works, cited contracts held by Meekatharra to sell about one million tonnes of pig iron a year to Indonesia from the planned new plant as helping underpin the economics of the proposed railway.
A Darwin-Alice Springs rail link would allow export of the pig iron to Meekatharra's two Indonesian partners in the new plant through the port of Darwin.

Indonesia's state-owned PT Krakatau Steel and privately-owned PT Maritosa Coalindo both now hold equity stakes of 15 percent in the South Australian Steel and Energy Project (SASE) proposed pig iron venture, Arthur said.
The two Indonesian partners are contributing a total of A$19 million to A$20 million to the project.
The proposed pig iron project did not depend on the Darwin railway going through, Arthur said.
Meekatharra planned to export through Whyalla or Port Pirie, near Adelaide, and would only export through Darwin if there was good economic reason to do so, he said.

However, whereas a previous federal government-backed study of the economics of the railway had found that pig iron and coal export traffic from Meekatharra would be fundamental to the rail project's success, later studies showed the railway viable even without the minerals traffic, he said.
"I believe that (the later study's finding) to be true," Arthur said.
Final feasibility studies on the pig iron plant will be conducted in parallel with construction and operation of the demonstration plant, expected to be operated for about six months, he said.
The demonstration plant's cost was still under examination but was believed to be less than A$10 million, he said.
